title: Magha Puja, deeper
hookLine: the verses taught that day: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind (Dhammapada 183–185)

cards: Sabbapapassa akaranam. On a full-moon night in Thailand, Laos or Cambodia, those Pali words may be chanted in a temple hall, the opening of a short verse.

In year one you met the night it remembers: the commentaries tell of twelve hundred and fifty monks who came to the Bamboo Grove near Rajagaha without being called, and of the Buddha giving them the whole teaching in three short verses.
You also met the first verse. Today, all three, and what the Long Discourses add about who speaks them.

teach.b: The three verses are known as the Ovada Patimokkha, the exhortation, and the Dhammapada keeps them as verses 183 to 185.
Here's the first, in Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Look at the middle phrase.
The Pali word Müller renders as good is kusala, which other translators give as skillful or wholesome. So the second move is more than being nice: it's taking up, on purpose, what actually helps.
The second verse, paraphrased, calls patience the highest austerity, and nirvana the highest thing of all. Someone who strikes or insults others, it adds, isn't a true renunciant, however they dress.
Patience sits where a reader might expect fasting or hardship.

teach.h: A SHORT LIST FOR A LIFE.
teach.b: The third verse is a short list: don't blame, don't strike, live restrained by the training, be moderate in food, sit and sleep in a quiet place, and give yourself to the higher mind.
Like the first verse, it begins with harm and ends with the mind. Now the Long Discourses.

teach.h: A PAST BUDDHA SAYS IT TOO.
teach.b: In the Mahapadana Sutta, Digha Nikaya 14, the Buddha tells of Vipassi, a Buddha of an age long past, gathering his monks and reciting these same verses.
So the teaching of all the Awakened is taken at its word: in that telling, this is what Buddhas say. Some teachers read the three moves as a ladder: restraint, then goodness, then a clear mind.
Others read them as one movement.
The verses set them side by side, short enough to chant in a breath, and the tradition hears in them the heart of it.

how: On Magha Puja, Theravada Buddhists in Thailand, Laos and Cambodia visit temples, keep precepts, listen to teachings and walk three times around a shrine at dusk carrying candles, incense and flowers; the Ovada Patimokkha verses are often chanted.

p: monks who came without being called

games.q: you are Vipassi, a Buddha of an age long past, and your monks have gathered before you. what do you give them?
o: a new teaching no one has heard before.
the same short verses: patience, no harm, the good, a clear mind.
nothing; you sit with them in silence.
games.why: in Digha Nikaya 14 he recites these same verses. the teaching of all the Awakened is shared, not invented fresh.

practice: Follow the breath in and out, and let the water settle: that's the clear mind of the first verse.
Then bring to mind one harm you could hold back from, a sharp word or a careless habit, and one good thing you could do, a call, a gift, a hand. Hold both simply, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Magha Puja. The full-moon day remembering the gathering of the twelve hundred and fifty, and the verses: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, the opening of Dhammapada 183: the not-doing of all evil.

carryVoice: Your line: the heart of it. Three moves, short enough for one breath. Until tomorrow.
